summary: A light has marked the Keweenaw Waterway's Lake Superior entrance since 1874. The current 1950 light stands 0.4 mile offshore on a breakwater; the Coast Guard has declared it excess.

light.note: Current light first lit 1950. The entrance has had a light since 20 November 1874 (Portage Lake Ship Canal Lighthouse, on the shore).

structures.type: steel tower, Streamlined Moderne, five stories
structures.note: The nomination gives a 50-foot steel tower; the whole structure stands about 110 feet above the lake bottom (about 33.5 m).

structures.type: rock-filled steel sheet-pile caisson, about 50 ft diameter
structures.material: steel sheet piling, rock fill, concrete deck
structures.status: standing, in about 30 ft of water

access.note: Coast Guard property, surrounded by water and reached by boat. Not open to public visitation. Visible from a parking area in McLain State Park (LighthouseFriends).

facts.agency: U.S. Coast Guard (owner until declared excess in 2025; offered by the General Services Administration)

events.note: Portage Lake Ship Canal Lighthouse: square tower on the gable end of a brick keeper's dwelling, west side of the canal entrance; deed obtained March 1874
First exhibited on the night of 20 November 1874 (LighthouseFriends)
Wooden pierhead tower on the west pier; light first exhibited 15 November 1879 (LighthouseFriends)
Steam fog signal for the canal pier authorised by the act of 15 February 1893; no appropriation yet (Board report)
Storm of 30 September 1894 carried away part of the elevated walk and the bridge at the canal pierhead; the bridge was rebuilt (Board FY1895 report)
Congress provided $5,500 for the fog signal on 2 March 1895 (LighthouseFriends)
Storm of 22 September 1895 washed fog-signal boilers and machinery into the canal; the Board FY1896 report confirms the loss and the recovery; wrecking crew from Marquette (LighthouseFriends)
New steam whistle in operation at the opening of navigation (LighthouseFriends)
Focal plane raised to 66 feet and the light's colour changed on 26 September 1896 (Board)
Arrowhead breakwaters completed to protect the entrance from Lake Superior (October 1901)
Illuminant changed from oil to incandescent oil vapour on 7 November 1912 (LighthouseFriends)
Fog signal moved from the west pier to the mainland near the main light (LighthouseFriends)
Fog signal changed to an air diaphone, two-second blast every twenty seconds (LighthouseFriends)
Old brick light demolished when the canal was widened; the archive gives 1935, LighthouseFriends 1937
Forty-six-foot skeletal tower erected on the shore site (LighthouseFriends)
Radiobeacon established nearby and a three-family keepers' dwelling completed (LighthouseFriends)
Entrance between the breakwaters widened by eighty feet (LighthouseFriends)
Current light established as a Federal aid to navigation on the breakwater end; steel caisson, concrete fog-signal building, steel tower
Aids to navigation automated during the 1970s (nomination)
National Register nomination received by the Park Service on 6 June 2014; listing status not confirmed in the sources read
GSA notice of availability (9 July 2025) for transfer to eligible entities under the National Historic Lighthouse Preservation Act; sixty days for letters of interest; no award found

corrections.why: The entrance has had a light since 20 November 1874 (Portage Lake Ship Canal Lighthouse, USLHS and LighthouseFriends). The 1950 light stands on the breakwater at the same entrance. Decide whether first_lit tracks the entrance or the current tower; the note field keeps both.

The nomination gives the light tower as steel and 50 feet tall (about 15.2 m). The whole structure is about 110 feet (about 33.5 m) from the lake bottom to the top of the tower. The 21.0 m figure matches neither.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The archive gives 1935 (canal widened, temporary building until the 1950 tower); LighthouseFriends gives 1937 for the replacement skeletal tower. The sources do not reconcile these dates.

The archive and LighthouseFriends list head keepers at the entrance until the 1960s, but the nomination says the light was initially operated remotely from shore by Coast Guard personnel. The sources do not reconcile the two accounts.

notes_for_editor: Duplicate records: data/stations has both us-mi-keweenaw-waterway-upper-entrance (this record, 1950 light) and us-mi-keweenaw-waterway-portage-river-upper-entrance-north-side (the archive's North Side record, est. 1950). They appear to describe the same light; flag for merging. The archive's North Side position (47.2400, -88.6248) is about 0.75 km from this record's position (47.2345, -88.6303); the archive's Portage Lake Ship Canal position (47.2319, -88.6283) is the 1874 entrance. Portage Lake Ship Canal place: the archive says 'discontinued 1935' and demolished 1935, yet its roster runs to 1958 (James E. Collins 1951-1958). Roster dates are NARA-based through the archive; LighthouseFriends lists the same names. Roster lines with 'at least' or no start year are kept as the archive prints them (to_approx / from_approx). The 'Portage Lake' name also belongs to Portage Lake Pierhead Range and Portage Lake Harbor on Lake Michigan: do not merge. The 1895 storm and boiler recovery are now confirmed by the Board's report for the fiscal year ended June 30, 1896 (scan p. 177 of annualreportlig02statgoog), which says the boilers and machinery were washed into the canal by the storm and recovered by a wrecking outfit from Marquette; the storm's date comes from LighthouseFriends (the OCR reads 'Beptember 22'). The Board's report for the fiscal year ended June 30, 1895 also records a storm of 30 September 1894 that carried away part of the pierhead walk and bridge (year inferred from the fiscal year). The NRHP nomination's 2014 listing status is not stated in the form text; the record's 2014 nrhp_listed should be checked against the NPS listing; the GSA notice of 2025 calls the light 'eligible for listing'. The record's characteristic 'Fl W 15s' matches the NRHP's white flash every 15 seconds; focal height 25 m matches LighthouseFriends' 82 ft. The NRHP's keepers statement (remote operation) conflicts with the archive and LighthouseFriends keeper lists for 1961-1963; no story claim depends on resolving this. Post-July-2025 transfer status: a websearch found news of the notice only; no award or transfer was found. The Coast Guard's disposal is not confirmed as complete. Newspapers: one Chronicling America search for 'Portage Lake' with 'fog signal' in Michigan papers, 1895-1896, returned no hits; the storm rests on the Board report plus LighthouseFriends. No newspaper search was run for the 1950 opening. The Keweenaw Portage River Light (1856-1920) is at the Lower Entrance end, not this station; it is mentioned in the story only as context. Fact-check 2026-10-27: the story's earlier statement that the Board's reports do not mention the storm was wrong and is corrected. The 1891 canal purchase ($350,000 'at a cost of') is on scan p. 547 as footnoted. The archive lists Susan Bennetts without a sex; the story no longer calls her a woman. Still open: printed page numbers for the 1896 and 1897 Board entries (the corpus gives scan pages only), and the 1950 North Side keepers versus the NRHP's remote-operation statement (left unreconciled, as before).
